comments.text: I'm near 70 years old and have been told by various dentist thru the decades that my teeth are in awful shape and I need urgent procedures done to save them. I have all my crooked teeth still.  My experience with dentistry is the same as my experience with car repair and commission mechanics. From a "sales" perspective their are questions to gauge how much the customer is willing/able to spend. When's the last time you visit a dentist? Do you floss after every meal? Filling a patient form that's like a credit app. Does the dentist really need those questions accurately answered? Why can't he just go by a thorough exam of the mouth. The population in the rest of the globe aren't walking around toothless by 40, or  having implants done. The last few years so much advertisement is for whole mouth implants. Geesh!  For a dentist, it must be a lot easier working on healthy mouths that don't need the procedure and reap the benefit of improving your skills while getting  paid for  your training venture.  The dentist educator, Elle Phillips, books and video's discusses reasonable low cost approach and makes more common sense than current American dental practice. It's gotten so bad that when I'm told I have more than 2 cavities I go to a different dentist for a check up.  I've notice in social media comments that now more and more dentist aren't discussing with the client what's needed they're just going a head and doing it the same day. It is not a requirement in many places to be a dentist to own a dental shop. I guess the term that describes this is private equity. If your a corporation you'll always be looking for people with the talent that attains confidence from the public fast, a top producer-compared to peers,. How it works:

A private equity firm identifies a hospital—often a community hospital in rural or underserved areas.

Because of that debt, (on the hospital not the firm) the hospital is forced to make quick cash to cover the interest payments.

Cost cutting measures take place: reduced salaries, staff levels cut & services scaled back

Nurses become overworked, support teams exhausted and care level drops.

Steward Health Care was purchased in 2010, Steward then expanded aggressively but filed for bankruptcy in 2024 with $9 billion of debt, after closing hospitals in Massachusetts and not paying vendors.
